chapters.title: Chapter 2: Intangible Assets: Brands, Patents, and Licences

lessons.title: Patents, Regulatory Licences, and Government-Granted Advantages

body.text: Some moats are dug by the company. Others are handed over by the law. A government-granted moat can be the widest of all, right up until the day the government changes its mind.

children.text: Brands earn their protection in the minds of customers. Patents and licences earn it in law. When the state says only a few companies may operate an exchange, rate bonds, hold depository accounts, or sell a patented drug, competition is not just difficult, it is illegal. That sounds like the perfect moat. For investors, it comes with three catches: it expires, it can be capped, and it can be taken back.
Patents: A Moat With a Built-In Expiry Date

A patent gives its owner the exclusive right to make and sell an invention for a fixed period. In India, under the Patents Act, 1970, that period is 20 years from the date of filing. Since 2005, India has granted product patents on pharmaceuticals, not just on manufacturing processes.

body.label: Patent term in India
body.value: 20 years from the date of filing
body.context: Not from the date the product reaches the market. Years spent in development and approval eat into the protected period.

body.title: How Long Is the Moat, Really?
body.prompt: A company files a patent application for a new drug molecule in January 2012. After clinical trials and regulatory approval, the drug launches in January 2021. Assuming a 20-year term from filing and no extensions, how many years of patent protection remain after launch?
body.explanation: The patent expires in January 2032, 20 years after filing. Launch in January 2021 leaves 11 years of protected sales. The headline 20-year term shrinks to roughly half once development time is counted.

children.text: What Happens When the Patent Expires

markDefs.definition: Chemically equivalent copies of a drug sold after the original patent expires, usually at a fraction of the branded price.
A US FDA incentive giving the first generic filer that challenges a patent (a "Paragraph IV" filing) six months in which no other generic can be approved, allowing higher prices during that window.

children.text: Most listed Indian pharma companies sit on the other side of this moat. They make
generics
, and a large part of their profit comes from launching in the US the moment a patent falls away. Under US rules, the first generic company to successfully challenge a patent can receive
180 days of exclusivity
before other generics can enter. That window can be enormously profitable, and then prices collapse.

body.title: Illustrative: Drug Price After Patent Expiry (Branded Price = 100)

children.text: The shape matters more than the exact figures, which vary drug by drug. Each new entrant pushes prices lower. A generic launch with exclusivity is a temporary moat measured in months, which is why the earnings of US-focused Indian generic makers can swing sharply from one year to the next.

markDefs.definition: Extending patent protection by patenting minor modifications of an existing drug, such as a new salt or crystal form.

children.text: Section 3(d) and evergreening.

Section 3(d) of the Patents Act blocks patents on new forms of known substances unless they show significantly enhanced efficacy. In 2013, the Supreme Court used it to reject Novartis's patent application for a form of its cancer drug Glivec. The provision limits
evergreening
, so innovators cannot easily stretch a moat beyond its original term in India.

markDefs.definition: Government permission for a company other than the patent holder to produce a patented product, usually on public health or affordability grounds, with a royalty paid to the patent holder.

children.text: Compulsory licences.
In 2012, India granted its first
compulsory licence
to Natco Pharma to make a generic version of Bayer's patented cancer drug Nexavar, on affordability grounds. A patent in India is strong, but not absolute.
Regulatory Licences: When Only a Few Are Allowed to Play

A licence moat exists when a regulator such as SEBI or the RBI limits who can operate in a business. Unlike a patent, a licence often has no expiry date. Its strength depends on how scarce the licences are and how much the regulator controls pricing.

body.caption: Licence moats in Indian listed markets, compared

cells: Only two in India: CDSL and NSDL
Very strong: a duopoly with high barriers and growing demat accounts
Few exchanges; MCX dominates commodity derivatives trading
Strong: licence plus liquidity network effects
A handful registered; reputation matters as much as the licence
Strong: licence plus decades of trust with bond investors
Over 40 AMCs hold mutual fund licences
Weak on its own: the licence is not scarce, so brand and distribution decide
Moderate: the licence is less scarce than it once was, so deposit franchise matters more
Strong but capped: AERA regulates aeronautical tariffs

body.text: A licence is a moat only if it is scarce. Holding a SEBI mutual fund licence tells you almost nothing about an AMC's competitive position, because dozens of rivals hold the same licence. Holding one of India's two depository licences tells you a great deal.

children.text: The Three Catches of Government-Granted Moats

columns.label: Catch 1: It expires
points: Development time shortens the useful period
Generic entry collapses prices once protection ends
Question to ask: how many protected years remain?

columns.label: Catch 2: It is capped
points: Regulators often control what licensed monopolies can charge
Airport aeronautical tariffs are set by AERA
Exchange and depository charges face SEBI scrutiny
Question to ask: who decides the price?

columns.label: Catch 3: It can be taken back
points: Policy can open a closed market overnight
Coal mining was opened to commercial private players in 2020
Licences can be cancelled for lapses
Question to ask: what would make the government change the rules?

children.text: Case Study: IRCTC and the Convenience Fee

IRCTC holds the Indian Railways mandate for online train ticketing, among other businesses, and earns a convenience fee on tickets booked through its platform. In late October 2021, the Ministry of Railways asked IRCTC to share 50% of that convenience fee revenue with it. The stock fell sharply in a single session. The decision was withdrawn the very next day, and the shares recovered much of the fall.

body.text: The IRCTC episode shows the defining risk of a government-granted moat: the same authority that grants the advantage decides how much of it the company keeps. The moat itself did not change that week. Who captured its value almost did. When the grantor is also a major shareholder or the counterparty, as the Railways is for IRCTC, that risk is ever present.

children.text: How to Evaluate a Licence or Patent Moat
Scarcity:
how many other companies hold the same licence or rights, and can the regulator easily grant more?
Duration:
for patents, how many years remain on the key products? For concessions, when does the agreement end and on what renewal terms?
Pricing freedom:
does a regulator cap fees or returns? Regulated returns protect downside but limit upside.
Policy risk:
is there a public interest argument for opening the market, cutting fees, or sharing revenue?
A second moat:
the strongest licence businesses layer trust, network effects, or scale on top of the licence, so they would stay strong even if more licences were issued.

body.title: Scarce or Not?
body.question: Which of these is the strongest licence-based moat?
options: A newly listed AMC with a SEBI mutual fund licence
A payments company with an RBI payment aggregator authorisation, one of dozens granted
One of only two depositories, with every demat account in the country held at either it or its rival
A small finance bank with an RBI licence operating in three states
body.explanation: Only option C combines extreme scarcity with a business every market participant needs. Mutual fund licences and payment aggregator authorisations are held by many companies. A small finance bank's licence is valuable, but many banks compete for the same deposits and borrowers.

body.title: Complete the Principle
body.textWithBlank: A regulatory licence is only a moat if it is ___, meaning few other companies can obtain the same permission.
body.explanation: If a regulator grants the same licence to dozens of companies, the licence is a requirement to compete, not a protection from competition.

body.title: The Toll Road Pitch
body.scenario: A friend recommends a listed infrastructure company that holds a 20-year concession to operate a busy toll road near Mumbai. There is no alternative route of similar quality. Toll rates rise each year based on a formula linked to wholesale inflation. The concession has 7 years left, and the company has not said whether it expects to win the renewal.
body.prompt: Evaluate this as a government-granted moat using scarcity, duration, pricing freedom, and policy risk.
body.modelAnswer: Scarcity is strong: no comparable route exists, so traffic has few alternatives. Pricing freedom is limited but predictable, since tolls rise with a formula rather than at the company's discretion, which protects against inflation but prevents premium pricing. Duration is the biggest problem: with only 7 years left and no clarity on renewal, this is a shrinking moat, and the business could be worth little after the concession ends unless it wins it again. Policy risk is real, since toll collection is politically sensitive and governments have in the past suspended or reduced tolls in response to public pressure. Before investing, you would want to value only the remaining 7 years of cash flows unless renewal terms are clear, check debt repayment against that shortened life, and not pay a multiple that assumes the moat lasts forever.

body.text: Companies named are used to illustrate concepts based on public information and are not investment recommendations. Regulatory frameworks change; check current SEBI, RBI, and ministry rules before relying on any detail.

points: Patents and regulatory licences create moats in law rather than in customers' minds
Indian patents last 20 years from filing, and development time means the useful protected period is often much shorter
Indian generic makers profit from patent expiries, but exclusivity windows are temporary and prices fall as more generics enter
Section 3(d) and compulsory licences mean patent moats in India are strong but not absolute
A licence is a moat only if it is scarce: CDSL's depository licence is, a mutual fund licence is not
Government-granted moats can expire, be price-capped, or be taken back, as the brief IRCTC convenience fee decision in 2021 showed
